Appendix Contents

Appendix A Derivation of the Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching Loss

This appendix provides a detailed derivation of the conditional uncertainty-aware flow matching loss ℒCUFM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}} by rewriting the unconditional Gaussian negative log-likelihood loss ℒUFM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} in terms of conditional flow matching. The key idea is to express expectations under the marginal distribution pt​(𝐱)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) using the conditional distribution pt​(𝐱∣𝐱1)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}), which enables tractable training despite the inaccessibility of the marginal velocity. For notational simplicity, time is uniformly sampled, i.e. t∼U⁡([0,1])t\sim U([0,1]), though any alternative time-sampling distribution could be used.

We begin by expanding the uncertainty-aware flow matching loss ℒUFM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} and decomposing it into four expectation terms, which will later be rewritten under the conditional distribution.

ℒUFM​(θ)=𝔼t,pt​(𝐱t)​[(u¯tθ​(𝐱t)−ut​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2+log⁡(σtθ​(𝐱t))]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\,\frac{\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big)^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big] (16)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼t,pt​(𝐱t)​[(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]⏟(A)−2​𝔼t,pt​(𝐱t)​[u¯tθ​(𝐱t)​ut​(𝐱t)2​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]⏟(B)\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t,\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\,\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big]}_{(A)}-2\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t,\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\,\frac{\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big]}_{(B)}
+\displaystyle+ 𝔼t,pt​(𝐱t)​[(ut​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]⏟(C)+𝔼t,pt​(𝐱t)​[log⁡(σtθ​(𝐱t))]⏟(D)\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t,\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\,\frac{(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big)^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big]}_{(C)}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t,\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\,\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big]}_{(D)}

Term (A) depends only on the predicted mean and variance and can be rewritten by expressing the marginal distribution pt​(𝐱t)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) as an integral over the conditional distribution pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) and the data distribution p1​(𝐱1)p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}).

(A)\displaystyle(A) =∫(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2​pt​(𝐱t)​d​𝐱t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})d\mathbf{x}_{t}dt (17)
=∫(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)​d​𝐱1​d​𝐱t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})d\mathbf{x}_{1}d\mathbf{x}_{t}dt
=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big]

Term (B) involves the cross term between the predicted mean and the true marginal velocity. Since the marginal velocity ut​(𝐱)u_{t}(\mathbf{x}) is intractable, we rewrite it using the law of total expectation under the conditional flow matching formulation.

(B)\displaystyle(B) =∫u¯tθ​(𝐱t)​ut​(𝐱t)2​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2​pt​(𝐱t)​d​𝐱t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int\frac{\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})d\mathbf{x}_{t}dt (18)
=∫u¯tθ​(𝐱t)2​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2​(∫ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)pt​(𝐱t)​d​𝐱1)​pt​(𝐱t)​d​𝐱t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int\frac{\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big(\int\frac{u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})}{p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}d\mathbf{x}_{1}\Big)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})d\mathbf{x}_{t}dt
=∫u¯tθ​(𝐱t)​ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)​d​𝐱1​d​𝐱t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int\frac{\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})d\mathbf{x}_{1}d\mathbf{x}_{t}dt
=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[u¯tθ​(𝐱t)​ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\frac{\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big]

By the same change of measure, terms (C) and (D) can be rewritten as

(C)=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[(ut​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2](C)=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\frac{(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}\Big] (19)
(D)=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[log⁡(σtθ​(𝐱t))](D)=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big] (20)

Therefore, ℒU​F​M​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{UFM}(\theta) can be rewritten as:

ℒUFM​(θ)=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))2−2​u¯tθ​(𝐱t)​ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)+(ut​(𝐱t))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2+log⁡(σtθ​(𝐱t))]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}-2\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})+(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big] (21)
=𝔼t,p1​(𝐱1),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​[(u¯tθ​(𝐱t)−ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1))2+(ut​(𝐱t))2−(ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1))22​(σtθ​(𝐱t))2+log⁡(σtθ​(𝐱t))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\,\frac{(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}))^{2}+(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}-(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}))^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big]

However, we cannot evaluate the true marginal velocity ut​(𝐱t)u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) in closed form. Using the identity in Equation 22, we can rewrite ut​(𝐱t)u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) as a ratio of expectations over 𝐱1∼p1\mathbf{x}_{1}\sim p_{1}:

ut​(𝐱t)\displaystyle u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) =∫ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)pt​(𝐱t)​d​𝐱1\displaystyle=\int\frac{u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})}{p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}d\mathbf{x}_{1} (22)
=∫ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)​d​𝐱1∫pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)​d​𝐱1\displaystyle=\frac{\int u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})d\mathbf{x}_{1}}{\int p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})d\mathbf{x}_{1}}
=𝔼p1​(𝐱1)​[ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)]𝔼p1​(𝐱1)​[pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)].\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})}[u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})]}{\mathbb{E}_{p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})}[p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})]}.

This suggests a self-normalized importance-sampling estimator based on a mini-batch {𝐱1,b}b=1B∼p1\{\mathbf{x}_{1,b}\}_{b=1}^{B}\sim p_{1}:

u^t​(𝐱t)=∑b=1But​(𝐱t∣𝐱1,b)​pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1,b)∑b=1Bpt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1,b).\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})\,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})}. (23)

Since ut​(𝐱t)u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) is intractable, we approximate (ut​(𝐱t))2(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2} by (u^t​(𝐱t))2(\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2} in our objective. This ratio-of-expectations naturally motivates an importance-weighted approximation, providing a tractable proxy for the unconditional target. Substituting u^t​(𝐱t)2\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2} yields the correction term Ut​(𝐱t,𝐱1):=u^t​(𝐱t)2−ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}):=\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2} and results in the conditional objective ℒCUFM​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}}(\theta) in Equation 2.

Remark on Jensen bias in approximating (ut​(𝐱t))2(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2} and why we still keep Ut​(𝐱t,𝐱1)U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}).

However, u^t​(𝐱t)2\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2} is not an unbiased estimator of ut​(𝐱t)2u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2} even when u^t​(𝐱t)\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) is a consistent proxy for ut​(𝐱t)u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). This follows from the identity 𝔼⁡[u^2]−(𝔼⁡[u^])2=Var⁡(u^)\mathbb{E}[\hat{u}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[\hat{u}])^{2}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{u}), i.e., squaring introduces a Jensen gap proportional to the estimator variance. Accordingly, the bias is controlled by the (mini-batch) estimator variance and typically decreases as the mini-batch size BB increases.

Despite this limitation, introducing the correction term Ut​(𝐱t,𝐱1):=u^t​(𝐱t)2−ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}):=\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2} still yields a closer surrogate to the original unconditional objective than omitting UtU_{t} altogether. Indeed, letting pt|1​(𝐱1∣𝐱t)=pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)​p1​(𝐱1)pt​(𝐱t)p_{t|1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})=\frac{p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})\,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1})}{p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})} denote the induced posterior in Equation 22, we have ut​(𝐱t)=𝔼p1|t​(𝐱1∣𝐱t)​[ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)]u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{p_{1|t}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})}[u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})] and thus

𝔼p1|t​(𝐱1∣𝐱t)​[ut​(𝐱t)2−ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2]=−Varp1|t​(𝐱1∣𝐱t)​(ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1))≤ 0.\mathbb{E}_{p_{1|t}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})}\!\left[u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2}\right]=-\,\mathrm{Var}_{p_{1|t}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})}\!\left(u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})\right)\ \leq\ 0.

Therefore, dropping UtU_{t} implicitly sets this negative term to zero, incurring a systematic bias that does not vanish with BB. In contrast, our proxy retains this variance-related correction up to the residual bias in u^t​(𝐱t)2\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}, which diminishes as the mini-batch estimator variance decreases (e.g., as BB increases).

Appendix B Details on Variance Propagation and Covariance Approximations

This appendix provides detailed derivations for the variance evolution equations and tractable approximations of the covariance between the state and the velocity field.

B.1 Derivations of the Mean and Variance Propagation Rules

Mean propagation (Equation 5).

Using the Gaussian velocity model utθ​(𝐱)=u¯tθ​(𝐱t)+σtθ​(𝐱t)⊙ϵu_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\odot\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), we have 𝔼⁡[utθ​(𝐱t)]=𝔼⁡[u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]\mathbb{E}[u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]=\mathbb{E}[\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]. Applying a first-order Taylor expansion of u¯tθ​(𝐱t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) around 𝐱¯t:=𝔼⁡[𝐱t]\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] yields

d​𝐱¯td​t=𝔼⁡[utθ​(𝐱t)]=𝔼⁡[u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]≈𝔼⁡[u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)+Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)]=u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t).\frac{d\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{dt}=\mathbb{E}\big[u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big]\approx\mathbb{E}\big[\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big]=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}). (24)
Variance propagation (Equation 6).

Under Euler integration between times tt and t+Δ​tt+\Delta t, the flow dynamics become

𝐱t+Δ​t=𝐱t+utθ​(𝐱t)​Δ​t.\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\,\Delta t. (25)

Applying the element-wise variance identity Var⁡(X+a​Y)=Var⁡(X)+a2​Var​(Y)+2​a​Cov​(X,Y)\mathrm{Var}(X+aY)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+a^{2}\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2a\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) to Equation 25 yields Equation 6, where Y=utθ​(𝐱t)Y=u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}).

Next, we justify the approximation Var⁡(utθ​(𝐱t))≈(σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2\mathrm{Var}(u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2} used in the main text. By the law of total variance and utθ​(𝐱t)=u¯tθ​(𝐱t)+σtθ​(𝐱t)⊙ϵu^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\odot\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), we have

Var⁡(utθ​(𝐱t))=\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))= 𝔼⁡[Var⁡(utθ​(𝐱t)∣𝐱t)]+Var⁡(𝔼⁡[utθ​(𝐱t)∣𝐱t])\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})]+\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]) (26)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼𝐱t​[(σtθ​(𝐱t))2]+Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\big[(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}\big]+\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))
≈\displaystyle\approx 𝔼𝐱t​[(σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2+∂(σtθ)2∂𝐱|𝐱¯t​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)]+Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\Big[(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}+\frac{\partial(\sigma^{\theta}_{t})^{2}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\Big|_{\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\Big]+\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))
=\displaystyle= (σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2+Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\displaystyle(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}+\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))

where the last step follows by dropping higher-order terms and using 𝔼⁡[𝐱t−𝐱¯t]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}]=0. The remaining term Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) captures variance induced by the spread of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. In principle, it can be estimated by Monte Carlo sampling: draw 𝐱t,i∼𝒩⁡(𝐱¯t,Var⁡[𝐱t])\mathbf{x}_{t,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t},\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]) and compute the empirical variance of u¯tθ​(𝐱t,i)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t,i}).

In the main text, we focus on the predicted heteroscedastic uncertainty and avoid this additional Monte Carlo overhead. Thus, we neglect Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) and use the approximation

Var⁡(utθ​(𝐱t))≈(σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2.\mathrm{Var}(u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}.

Section H.1 further shows that explicitly including Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) has negligible empirical effect on the resulting uncertainty estimates.

Taylor covariance approximation (Equation 7).

We write utθ​(𝐱t)=u¯tθ​(𝐱t)+σtθ​(𝐱t)⊙ϵu^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\odot\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). The noise term does not contribute to the covariance because ϵ\epsilon is independent of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and has zero mean. Thus,

Cov⁡(𝐱t,utθ​(𝐱t))\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) =𝔼⁡[𝐱t⊙utθ​(𝐱t)]−𝔼⁡[𝐱t]⊙𝔼⁡[utθ​(𝐱t)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]-\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]\odot\mathbb{E}[u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})] (27)
=𝔼𝐱t​[𝐱t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]−𝐱¯t⊙𝔼𝐱t​[u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\odot\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]
≈𝔼𝐱t​[𝐱t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]−𝐱¯t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t).\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}).

Applying a first-order Taylor expansion of u¯tθ​(𝐱t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) around 𝐱¯t\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} gives

𝔼𝐱t​[𝐱t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\big[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big] ≈𝔼𝐱t​[𝐱t⊙(u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)+Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t))]\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\Big[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\,(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big)\Big] (28)
=𝐱¯t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)+𝔼𝐱t​[(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)⊙(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t))].\displaystyle=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\Big[(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\odot\big(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\,(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big)\Big].

To keep the propagation tractable in high dimensions, we approximate Cov⁡(𝐱t)∈ℝn×n\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} as diagonal (i.e., we neglect off-diagonal entries). Then the ii-th element of the last expectation becomes

𝔼⁡[(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)i​(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t))i]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})_{i}\,\big(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\,(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big)_{i}\Big] =∑j=1n(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))i​j​𝔼​[(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)i​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)j]\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))_{ij}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})_{i}\,(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})_{j}\Big] (29)
=∑j=1n(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))i​j​(Cov⁡(𝐱t))i​j=(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))i​i​Var​[𝐱t]i.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))_{ij}\,(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))_{ij}=(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))_{ii}\,\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]_{i}.

Therefore,

𝔼𝐱t​[𝐱t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱t)]≈𝐱¯t⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)+diag⁡(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t].\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\big[\mathbf{x}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big]\approx\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]. (30)

Combining Equations 27, 28, 29 and 30 yields Equation 7.

Jacobian vector product approximation (Equation 8).

Let 𝐫∈ℝn\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be a Rademacher vector with independent entries sampled uniformly from {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}, so that 𝔼⁡[ri​rj]=δi​j\mathbb{E}[r_{i}r_{j}]=\delta_{ij}. Define 𝝈tx:=Var⁡[𝐱t]\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{x}:=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]} and 𝐯:=𝝈tx⊙𝐫\mathbf{v}:=\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{x}\odot\mathbf{r}. Then, for each coordinate ii,

𝔼⁡[vi​(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​𝐯)i]=∑j=1n(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))i​j​𝔼​[vi​vj]=(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))i​i​(𝝈tx)i2,\mathbb{E}\big[v_{i}(J_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\mathbf{v})_{i}\big]=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(J_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))_{ij}\,\mathbb{E}[v_{i}v_{j}]=(J_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))_{ii}\,(\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{x})_{i}^{2},

since 𝔼⁡[vi​vj]=(𝝈tx)i​(𝝈tx)j​𝔼​[ri​rj]\mathbb{E}[v_{i}v_{j}]=(\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{x})_{i}(\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{x})_{j}\,\mathbb{E}[r_{i}r_{j}] and 𝔼⁡[ri​rj]=δi​j\mathbb{E}[r_{i}r_{j}]=\delta_{ij}. Stacking all coordinates gives

𝔼⁡[𝐯⊙(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​𝐯)]=diag⁡(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t].\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{v}\odot(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\mathbf{v})\big]=\mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]. (31)

Therefore, Equation 8 provides an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of diag⁡(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t]\mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] using only Jacobian–vector products.

B.2 Approximations of Cov⁡(𝐱t,utθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))

We approximate Cov⁡(𝐱t,utθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) in three tractable ways:

Cov⁡(𝐱t,utθ​(𝐱t))≈{0(Option 1)1S​∑i=1S(𝝈tx⊙𝐫i)⊙(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t)​(𝝈tx⊙𝐫i))(Option 2)1S​∑i=1S𝐱t,i⊙u¯tθ​(𝐱t,i)−𝐱¯t⊙(1S​∑i=1Su¯tθ​(𝐱t,i))(Option 3)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx\begin{cases}0&(\text{Option 1})\\[5.69054pt] \frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}(\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r}_{i})\odot\Big(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})(\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r}_{i})\Big)&(\text{Option 2})\\[5.69054pt] \frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{x}_{t,i}\odot\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t,i})-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\odot\Big(\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t,i})\Big)&(\text{Option 3})\\ \end{cases} (32)

where 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} are Rademacher vectors and 𝐱t,i∼𝒩⁡(𝐱¯t,diag⁡(Var⁡[𝐱t]))\mathbf{x}_{t,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t},\mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}])). Here SS denotes the number of samples.

Option 1. Ignore the covariance term. This is the cheapest choice computationally, but it discards the interaction between state and flow.

Option 2. This is the estimator deployed in our implementation. It estimates diag⁡(Jtθ​(𝐱¯t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t]\mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] using SS Rademacher probes and Jacobian-vector products; see Algorithm 1 for details.

Option 3. A Monte Carlo alternative, similar to BayesDiff (Kou et al., 2023), draws 𝐱t,i∼𝒩⁡(𝐱¯t,Var⁡[𝐱t])\mathbf{x}_{t,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t},\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]) for i=1,⋯,Si=1,\cdots,S and estimates the covariance directly from sample moments.

Appendix C Variance Propagation under Heun’s 2nd-Order Sampling

This appendix extends the variance propagation rule of Appendix B from the Euler discretization to Heun’s 2nd-order integrator. We follow the same conventions as in the main text: all operations are element-wise, Var⁡[⋅]\mathrm{Var}[\cdot] and Cov⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{Cov}(\cdot,\cdot) denote the element-wise (diagonal) variance and covariance, and the Gaussian velocity model is utθ​(𝐱)=u¯tθ​(𝐱)+σtθ​(𝐱)⊙ϵu^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\odot\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).

Heun’s 2nd-order update.

Given a step size Δ​t\Delta t, Heun’s 2nd-order (Heun2) method uses one Euler predictor and a trapezoidal corrector:

𝐤1\displaystyle\mathbf{k}_{1} =utθ​(𝐱t)=u¯tθ​(𝐱t)+σtθ​(𝐱t)⊙ϵ1,\displaystyle=\;u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\;=\;\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\odot\epsilon_{1}, (33)
𝐱~t+Δ​t\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t} =𝐱t+𝐤1​Δ​t,\displaystyle=\;\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{k}_{1}\,\Delta t,
𝐤2\displaystyle\mathbf{k}_{2} =ut+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~t+Δ​t)=u¯t+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~t+Δ​t)+σt+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~t+Δ​t)⊙ϵ2,\displaystyle=\;u^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t})\;=\;\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t})+\sigma^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t})\odot\epsilon_{2},
𝐱t+Δ​t\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t} =𝐱t+Δ​t2​(𝐤1+𝐤2),\displaystyle=\;\mathbf{x}_{t}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\big(\mathbf{k}_{1}+\mathbf{k}_{2}\big),

with independent ϵ1,ϵ2∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) sampled at the two stages.

For notational brevity we define the Euler-predicted mean state

𝐱~¯t+Δ​t:=𝔼⁡[𝐱~t+Δ​t]≈𝐱¯t+u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)​Δ​t,\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t}\;:=\;\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t}]\;\approx\;\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\,\Delta t, (34)

which follows from the same linearization as in Equation 24, and abbreviate

σ1:=σtθ​(𝐱¯t),σ2:=σt+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~¯t+Δ​t),J1:=Jtθ​(𝐱¯t),J2:=Jt+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~¯t+Δ​t).\sigma_{1}:=\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}),\quad\sigma_{2}:=\sigma^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t}),\quad J_{1}:=J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}),\quad J_{2}:=J^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t}).
Mean dynamics.

Applying a first-order Taylor expansion of u¯tθ\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t} around 𝐱¯t\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} (as in Equation 24) to both stages of Equation 33 yields

𝐱¯t+Δ​t≈𝐱¯t+Δ​t2​(u¯tθ​(𝐱¯t)+u¯t+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~¯t+Δ​t)),\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t}\;\approx\;\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\Big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t})\Big), (35)

which is exactly the deterministic Heun step applied to the mean state.

Variance decomposition.

Applying the element-wise variance identity to 𝐱t+Δ​t=𝐱t+Δ​t2​(𝐤1+𝐤2)\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\mathbf{k}_{1}+\mathbf{k}_{2}) gives the exact decomposition

Var⁡[𝐱t+Δ​t]=\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}]\;= Var⁡[𝐱t]+(Δ​t)24​(Var⁡[𝐤1]+Var⁡[𝐤2]+2​Cov​(𝐤1,𝐤2))\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]+\tfrac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{4}\Big(\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{1}]+\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{2}]+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2})\Big) (36)
+Δ​t​(Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤1)+Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)).\displaystyle+\Delta t\,\Big(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1})+\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2})\Big).

Compared with the Euler rule (Equation 6), Equation 36 introduces two additional variance terms (Var⁡[𝐤2]\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{2}] and Cov⁡(𝐤1,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2})) and one additional state–velocity coupling term (Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2})), all arising from the corrector stage. We now derive tractable approximations for each term.

Stage variances.

Var⁡[𝐤1]\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{1}]. By the law of total variance and a first-order Taylor expansion of σtθ\sigma^{\theta}_{t} around 𝐱¯t\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} (identical to Equation 26), and neglecting Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})),

Var⁡[𝐤1]≈σ12.\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{1}]\;\approx\;\sigma_{1}^{2}. (37)

Var⁡[𝐤2]\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{2}]. Applying the law of total variance to 𝐤2|𝐱~t+Δ​t\mathbf{k}_{2}\mid\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t} yields

Var⁡[𝐤2]=𝔼𝐱~​[σt+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~)2]+Var⁡(u¯t+Δ​tθ​(𝐱~)).\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{2}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}\big[\sigma^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})^{2}\big]+\mathrm{Var}\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})\big).

A first-order Taylor expansion of σt+Δ​tθ\sigma^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t} around 𝐱~¯t+Δ​t\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t}, combined with the same neglect-of-Var-of-mean step, gives

Var⁡[𝐤2]≈σ22.\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{k}_{2}]\;\approx\;\sigma_{2}^{2}. (38)

The only change relative to Equation 37 is that σ22\sigma_{2}^{2} is evaluated at the Euler-predicted mean 𝐱~¯t+Δ​t\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t} and at time t+Δ​tt+\Delta t.

State–velocity covariances.

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤1)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1}). This term is identical to the Euler case in Equations 7 and 8: it approximates diag⁡(J1)⊙Var⁡[𝐱t]\mathrm{diag}(J_{1})\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] via Hutchinson’s estimator. With 𝝈tx:=Var⁡[𝐱t]\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}:=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]} and SS independent Rademacher probes 𝐫i∈ℝn\mathbf{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} whose entries are i.i.d. uniform on {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}, defining the scaled probes 𝐯i:=𝝈tx⊙𝐫i\mathbf{v}_{i}:=\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r}_{i},

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤1)≈1S​∑i=1S𝐯i⊙(J1​𝐯i).\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1})\;\approx\;\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot(J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i}). (39)

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2}). Expand u¯t+Δ​tθ\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t+\Delta t} around 𝐱~¯t+Δ​t\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t} and write the predictor perturbation as

𝐱~t+Δ​t−𝐱~¯t+Δ​t≈(I+J1​Δ​t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)+σ1⊙ϵ1​Δ​t.\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t+\Delta t}-\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}}_{t+\Delta t}\;\approx\;(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\sigma_{1}\odot\epsilon_{1}\,\Delta t. (40)

Since ϵ1,ϵ2\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2} are zero-mean and independent of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, the noise terms do not contribute to Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2}). Applying the same diagonal-Cov⁡(𝐱t)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) approximation as in Equations 29 and 30,

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)≈diag⁡(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t].\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2})\;\approx\;\mathrm{diag}\!\big(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)\big)\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]. (41)

Cov⁡(𝐤1,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2}). Using the first-order expansions

𝐤1−𝐤¯1≈J1​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)+σ1⊙ϵ1,\mathbf{k}_{1}-\bar{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\;\approx\;J_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\sigma_{1}\odot\epsilon_{1}, (42)
𝐤2−𝐤¯2≈J2​((I+J1​Δ​t)​(𝐱t−𝐱¯t)+σ1⊙ϵ1​Δ​t)+σ2⊙ϵ2,\mathbf{k}_{2}-\bar{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\;\approx\;J_{2}\big((I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\sigma_{1}\odot\epsilon_{1}\,\Delta t\big)+\sigma_{2}\odot\epsilon_{2}, (43)

and the mutual independence of 𝐱t,ϵ1,ϵ2\mathbf{x}_{t},\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}, the element-wise cross-covariance at coordinate ii splits into a state-driven and a noise-driven part. Under the diagonal-Cov⁡(𝐱t)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) approximation, a direct computation (cf. Equation 29) gives

Cov​(𝐤1,𝐤2)i≈∑j=1n(J1)i​j​(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t))i​j​Var​[𝐱t]j⏟state-driven+Δ​t​(J2)i​i​(σ1)i2⏟noise-driven,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2})_{i}\;\approx\;\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{n}(J_{1})_{ij}\big(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)\big)_{ij}\,\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]_{j}}_{\text{state-driven}}\;+\;\underbrace{\Delta t\,(J_{2})_{ii}\,(\sigma_{1})_{i}^{2}}_{\text{noise-driven}}, (44)

or equivalently in matrix form,

Cov⁡(𝐤1,𝐤2)≈diag⁡(J1​diag​(Var⁡[𝐱t])​(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t))⊤)+Δ​t​diag​(J2)⊙σ12.\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2})\;\approx\;\mathrm{diag}\!\big(J_{1}\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}])\,(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t))^{\top}\big)\;+\;\Delta t\,\mathrm{diag}(J_{2})\odot\sigma_{1}^{2}. (45)

Unlike Equation 41, the state-driven part of Equation 44 is not of the form diag⁡(M)⊙Var⁡[𝐱t]\mathrm{diag}(M)\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] for a single matrix MM, because the two velocity stages are linearly mapped by different Jacobians. A Hutchinson estimator that respects this structure is derived below.

Hutchinson–JVP estimators.

Explicitly forming J1J_{1} or J2J_{2} is intractable in high dimensions. We therefore estimate the diagonal Jacobian products appearing in Equations 39, 41 and 45 via Rademacher probes and Jacobian–vector products, following the same strategy as Equation 8.

Setup. Let 𝝈tx:=Var⁡[𝐱t]\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}:=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]}, and draw two independent Rademacher vectors 𝐫,𝐫′∈ℝn\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} whose entries are i.i.d. uniform on {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}, so that

𝔼⁡[ri​rj]=𝔼⁡[ri′​rj′]=δi​j,𝔼⁡[ri​rj′]= 0.\mathbb{E}[r_{i}r_{j}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}[r^{\prime}_{i}r^{\prime}_{j}]\;=\;\delta_{ij},\qquad\mathbb{E}[r_{i}r^{\prime}_{j}]\;=\;0. (46)

Define the scaled probes

𝐯:=𝝈tx⊙𝐫,𝐰:=σ1⊙𝐫′,\mathbf{v}\;:=\;\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r},\qquad\mathbf{w}\;:=\;\sigma_{1}\odot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}, (47)

which satisfy 𝔼⁡[vi​vj]=Var​[𝐱t]i​δi​j\mathbb{E}[v_{i}v_{j}]=\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]_{i}\,\delta_{ij} and 𝔼⁡[wi​wj]=(σ1)i2​δi​j\mathbb{E}[w_{i}w_{j}]=(\sigma_{1})_{i}^{2}\,\delta_{ij}.

Derivation of the Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2}) estimator. Let M:=J2​(I+J1​Δ​t)M:=J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t). At coordinate ii,

𝔼⁡[vi​(M​𝐯)i]=∑j=1nMi​j​𝔼​[vi​vj]=Mi​i​Var​[𝐱t]i.\mathbb{E}\big[v_{i}\,(M\mathbf{v})_{i}\big]\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}M_{ij}\,\mathbb{E}[v_{i}v_{j}]\;=\;M_{ii}\,\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]_{i}. (48)

Stacking all coordinates yields

𝔼𝐫​[𝐯⊙(M​𝐯)]=diag⁡(M)⊙Var⁡[𝐱t]=diag⁡(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t))⊙Var⁡[𝐱t],\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}}\!\big[\mathbf{v}\odot(M\mathbf{v})\big]\;=\;\mathrm{diag}(M)\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]\;=\;\mathrm{diag}\!\big(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)\big)\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}], (49)

which matches Equation 41. The product M​𝐯=J2​(𝐯+J1​𝐯​Δ​t)M\mathbf{v}=J_{2}(\mathbf{v}+J_{1}\,\mathbf{v}\,\Delta t) is computed via two Jacobian–vector products, avoiding explicit formation of J1,J2J_{1},J_{2}, or MM. Using SS i.i.d. probes {𝐫i}\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\} gives the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤2)≈1S​∑i=1S𝐯i⊙(J2​(𝐯i+J1​𝐯i​Δ​t)).\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2})\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot\Big(J_{2}(\mathbf{v}_{i}+J_{1}\,\mathbf{v}_{i}\,\Delta t)\Big). (50)

Setting J2=IJ_{2}=I and Δ​t=0\Delta t=0 recovers the Euler-case estimator Equation 8 for Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤1)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1}),

Cov⁡(𝐱t,𝐤1)≈1S​∑i=1S𝐯i⊙(J1​𝐯i).\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1})\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot(J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i}). (51)

Derivation of the Cov⁡(𝐤1,𝐤2)\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2}) estimator. We treat the state-driven and noise-driven parts of Equation 44 separately.

State-driven part. Let A:=J1A:=J_{1} and B:=J2​(I+J1​Δ​t)B:=J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t). Using Equation 46,

𝔼⁡[(A​𝐯)i​(B​𝐯)i]=∑j,k=1nAi​j​Bi​k​𝔼​[vj​vk]=∑j=1nAi​j​Bi​j​Var​[𝐱t]j,\mathbb{E}\big[(A\mathbf{v})_{i}\,(B\mathbf{v})_{i}\big]\;=\;\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}A_{ij}\,B_{ik}\,\mathbb{E}[v_{j}v_{k}]\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}\,B_{ij}\,\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]_{j}, (52)

which coincides with the state-driven part of Equation 44 coordinate by coordinate. Thus, stacking over ii,

𝔼𝐫​[(J1​𝐯)⊙(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t)​𝐯)]=diag⁡(J1​diag​(Var⁡[𝐱t])​(J2​(I+J1​Δ​t))⊤).\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}}\!\big[(J_{1}\mathbf{v})\odot(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t)\mathbf{v})\big]\;=\;\mathrm{diag}\!\big(J_{1}\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}])\,(J_{2}(I+J_{1}\,\Delta t))^{\top}\big). (53)

Noise-driven part. Using 𝔼⁡[wi​wj]=(σ1)i2​δi​j\mathbb{E}[w_{i}w_{j}]=(\sigma_{1})_{i}^{2}\,\delta_{ij},

𝔼⁡[wi​(J2​𝐰)i]=∑j=1n(J2)i​j​𝔼​[wi​wj]=(J2)i​i​(σ1)i2.\mathbb{E}\big[w_{i}\,(J_{2}\mathbf{w})_{i}\big]\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}(J_{2})_{ij}\,\mathbb{E}[w_{i}w_{j}]\;=\;(J_{2})_{ii}\,(\sigma_{1})_{i}^{2}. (54)

Stacking over ii gives

𝔼𝐫′​[𝐰⊙(J2​𝐰)]=diag⁡(J2)⊙σ12,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\!\big[\mathbf{w}\odot(J_{2}\mathbf{w})\big]\;=\;\mathrm{diag}(J_{2})\odot\sigma_{1}^{2}, (55)

which matches the noise-driven term of Equation 44.

Combined estimator. Drawing SS independent probe pairs {(𝐫i,𝐫i′)}i=1S\{(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{S} and combining Equations 53 and 55 yields the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator

Cov⁡(𝐤1,𝐤2)≈1S​∑i=1S(J1​𝐯i)⊙(J2​(𝐯i+J1​𝐯i​Δ​t))+Δ​tS​∑i=1S𝐰i⊙(J2​𝐰i).\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2})\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}(J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i})\odot\Big(J_{2}(\mathbf{v}_{i}+J_{1}\,\mathbf{v}_{i}\,\Delta t)\Big)\;+\;\tfrac{\Delta t}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{w}_{i}\odot(J_{2}\mathbf{w}_{i}). (56)

Computational cost and probe sharing. The three estimators Equations 51, 50 and 56 can share the probes {𝐫i}\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\} and cache the intermediate products {J1​𝐯i,𝐯i,+Δ​t​J1​𝐯i}\{J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i},\,\mathbf{v}_{i},+\Delta tJ_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i}\} across terms. Per sampling step, the total overhead is one JVPs with J1J_{1} (for J1​𝐯iJ_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i}) and two JVPs with J2J_{2} (for J2​(𝐯i,+Δ​t​J1​𝐯i)J_{2}(\mathbf{v}_{i},+\Delta tJ_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i}), and J2​𝐰iJ_{2}\mathbf{w}_{i}).

Final Heun2 variance propagation rule.

Substituting Equations 37, 38, 51, 50 and 56 into Equation 36 yields the Heun2 variance update directly in Hutchinson/JVP form:

Var⁡[𝐱t+Δ​t]≈\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}]\;\approx Var⁡[𝐱t]+(Δ​t)24​(σ12+σ22)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]\;+\;\tfrac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{4}\big(\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}\big) (57)
+Δ​tS∑i=1S𝐯i⊙(J1𝐯i)\displaystyle+\tfrac{\Delta t}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot(J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i})
+Δ​tS∑i=1S𝐯i⊙(J2(𝐯i+ΔtJ1𝐯i))\displaystyle+\tfrac{\Delta t}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot\Big(J_{2}(\mathbf{v}_{i}+\Delta t\,J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i})\Big)
+(Δ​t)22​S∑i=1S(J1𝐯i)⊙(J2(𝐯i+ΔtJ1𝐯i))\displaystyle+\tfrac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{2S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}(J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i})\odot\Big(J_{2}(\mathbf{v}_{i}+\Delta t\,J_{1}\mathbf{v}_{i})\Big)
+(Δ​t)32​S∑i=1S𝐰i⊙(J2𝐰i).\displaystyle+\tfrac{(\Delta t)^{3}}{2S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}\mathbf{w}_{i}\odot(J_{2}\mathbf{w}_{i}).

The first line is the trapezoidal injected-noise term, while the remaining three probe averages estimate Δ​t​Cov​(𝐱t,𝐤1)\Delta t\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{1}), Δ​t​Cov​(𝐱t,𝐤2)\Delta t\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{2}), and (Δ​t)22​Cov​(𝐤1,𝐤2)\tfrac{(\Delta t)^{2}}{2}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2}), respectively. Expanding the compact JVP products recover the matrix-form expressions in Equations 41 and 45, including the 𝒪⁡(Δ​t)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t), 𝒪⁡(Δ​t2)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{2}), and 𝒪⁡(Δ​t3)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3}) contributions discussed above.

Appendix D Derivations of λ∗\lambda^{*}

Recall that UCFG chooses a scalar CFG scale λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 by minimizing the total predicted variance of the extrapolated velocity. Using the notation in Section 3.3, let σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)∈ℝn\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and σt,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)∈ℝn\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the element-wise standard deviations of the conditional and unconditional velocities, respectively. As described in Equation 13, the element-wise standard deviation of the extrapolated velocity is

σ~​(λ)=(1+λ)​σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)−λ​σt,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)=σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+λ⁡(σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)−σt,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)).\tilde{\sigma}(\lambda)=(1+\lambda)\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\lambda\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})=\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\lambda(\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})). (58)

Therefore, Equation 15 can be written as the following least-squares problem:

λopt=arg⁡min⁡∑i=1nλ≥0⁡σ~i​(λ)2=arg⁡minλ≥0​‖σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+λ​𝐝‖22,𝐝:=σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)−σt,∅θ​(𝐱¯t).\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=\arg\min_{\lambda\geq 0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\sigma}_{i}(\lambda)^{2}=\arg\min_{\lambda\geq 0}\|\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\lambda\mathbf{d}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{d}:=\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}). (59)

Expanding the objective yields a convex quadratic in λ\lambda:

J⁡(λ)=‖σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+λ​𝐝‖22=σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)⊤​σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+2​λ​𝐝⊤​σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+λ2​𝐝⊤​𝐝.J(\lambda)=\|\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\lambda\mathbf{d}\|_{2}^{2}=\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})^{\top}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+2\lambda\,\mathbf{d}^{\top}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\lambda^{2}\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{d}. (60)

When 𝐝⊤​𝐝>0\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{d}>0, the unconstrained minimizer is obtained by setting d​Jd​λ=0\frac{dJ}{d\lambda}=0:

d​Jd​λ=2​𝐝⊤​σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)+2​λ​𝐝⊤​𝐝=0⟹λ⋆=−𝐝⊤​σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)𝐝⊤​𝐝=(σt,∅θ)⊤​σt,yθ−‖σt,yθ‖22‖σt,yθ−σt,∅θ‖22.\frac{dJ}{d\lambda}=2\,\mathbf{d}^{\top}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+2\lambda\,\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda^{\star}=-\frac{\mathbf{d}^{\top}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})}{\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{d}}=\frac{(\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing})^{\top}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}-\|\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}-\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}\|_{2}^{2}}. (61)

Imposing the constraint λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 gives the closed-form solution:

λopt=max⁡(0,λ⋆).\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=\max(0,\lambda^{\star}). (62)

If 𝐝⊤​𝐝=0\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0 (i.e., 𝝈y=𝝈∅\bm{\sigma}_{y}=\bm{\sigma}_{\varnothing}), the objective J⁡(λ)J(\lambda) is constant in λ\lambda, and we set λopt=0\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=0. Finally, we apply the clamp in Equation 14:

λ∗=min⁡(λopt,λmax).\lambda^{\ast}=\min(\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}},\lambda_{\max}).

Appendix E Implementation Details

E.1 Model & Training

Architectures.

For CIFAR-10, we use an ADM-based unconditional flow matching model. The architectural configuration follows standard ADM design choices and is detailed in Table 9. For ImageNet-128 and ImageNet-256, we adopt DiT-based conditional latent flow matching models, as described in Section 4, using DiT-B/2 as the backbone and a pretrained autoencoder to map RGB images to a latent space.

Training procedure.

We summarize the training hyper-parameters for all datasets in Table 8. All models are trained with EMA, using the decay rates reported in the table. For CIFAR-10, we employ a skewed time-step sampling strategy used in EDM (Karras et al., 2022) during training. For ImageNet-256, we train the model using reverse-time parameterization, consistent with the pretrained latent flow matching setup.

For datasets involving fine-tuning, we apply linear gradient warm-up for the specified number of steps and use gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 1.0. Batch sizes and the number of GPUs used for each setting are reported in Table 8. For the reweighted mini-batch estimator used to compute u^t\hat{u}_{t}, the batch size is defined per GPU and aggregated across devices during training.

Hardware.

All training, fine-tuning, and TFLOPs-based compute measurements are run on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs (48 GB memory); the GPU counts reported in Table 8 refer to this hardware. A subset of inference runs (sampling and evaluation that does not contribute to the TFLOPs measurements) is additionally executed on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU.

Uncertainty modeling.

For uncertainty-aware training, we add a variance prediction head to the pretrained flow matching backbone. The variance head predicts log⁡σ\log\sigma to improve numerical stability during training. We use the β\beta-NLL (Seitzer et al., 2022) objective with β=1.0\beta=1.0 for all experiments.

For ImageNet-128 and ImageNet-256, classifier-free conditioning is enabled by applying label dropout with probability 0.1 during training.

E.2 Flow Matching Versions of Baselines

Existing uncertainty quantification methods for sampling-based generative models are primarily developed for diffusion models. To enable a fair comparison with UA-Flow, we adapt these baselines (De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025; Kou et al., 2023; Jazbec et al., 2025) to the flow matching framework. In this subsection, we describe how the diffusion-based formulations of these methods are converted into their flow matching counterparts.

Aleatoric Uncertainty (AU) (De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025).

In the original formulation, Aleatoric Uncertainty (AU) estimates sample uncertainty using the score function of a diffusion model. At each sampling step tt, the model first estimates the clean data sample 𝐱^1\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1} from the predicted score ϵtθ​(𝐱t)\epsilon_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). Multiple perturbed states 𝐱^ti\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{\,i} are then generated by re-noising the estimated data, and the variance of the score predictions ϵtθ​(𝐱^ti)\epsilon_{t}^{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{\,i}) is used as a measure of sample uncertainty.

To adapt AU to flow matching, we replace the score function with the learned velocity field utθ​(𝐱t)u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). Assuming an affine probability path, the clean data estimate 𝐱^1\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1} can be recovered from the current state 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and the predicted velocity as

𝐱^1=1α˙t​βt−β˙t​αt​(−β˙t​𝐱t+βt​utθ​(𝐱t)).\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\dot{\alpha}_{t}\beta_{t}-\dot{\beta}_{t}\alpha_{t}}\left(-\dot{\beta}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\beta_{t}u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right). (63)

Starting from the estimated data 𝐱^1\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1}, we generate multiple perturbed states 𝐱^ti\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{\,i} by applying the forward affine transformation. We then compute the element-wise variance of the velocity predictions utθ​(𝐱^ti)u_{t}^{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{\,i}), which serves as the aleatoric uncertainty estimate at time tt. We aggregate the element-wise velocity variances over the late-stage sampling steps to obtain a sample uncertainty map, which is reduced to a scalar score for filtering as described in Section 4.2.

BayesDiff (Kou et al., 2023).

In the diffusion-based formulation, BayesDiff estimates the uncertainty of the score function at each sampling step using Laplace Last Layer Approximation (LLLA) (Daxberger et al., 2021). The estimated score variance is then propagated through the diffusion dynamics to obtain uncertainty estimates for the generated samples.

To adapt BayesDiff to flow matching, we apply LLLA to the velocity field and estimate the variance of the predicted velocity at each time step. This velocity variance is subsequently propagated through the flow dynamics following the same uncertainty propagation scheme as in the original BayesDiff formulation.

Generative Uncertainty (GenUnc) (Jazbec et al., 2025).

In the diffusion-based formulation, Generative Uncertainty (GenUnc) estimates sample uncertainty by sampling multiple model weights through LLLA and generating multiple images from the same noise realization. The resulting images are embedded into the CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) feature space, and the entropy of the extracted features is used as a sample-level uncertainty score.

For flow matching, we follow the same procedure by sampling model weights, generating multiple samples from the same initial noise using the corresponding flow matching model, and computing the variance of the resulting CLIP features as the sample-level uncertainty score.

E.3 APG and APG+UCFG for Flow Matching

We adapt adaptive projected guidance (APG) (Sadat et al., 2024) to flow matching by operating directly on the conditional and unconditional mean velocities. Using the notation in Section 3.3, let u¯t,yθ​(𝐱¯t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) and u¯t,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) denote the conditional and unconditional mean velocities, respectively. For brevity, we suppress their dependence on 𝐱¯t\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} and define the CFG direction

gt=u¯t,yθ−u¯t,∅θ.g_{t}=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}-\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}. (64)
APG.

Following APG, we first apply reverse momentum:

mt=gt+β​mt−1,m_{t}=g_{t}+\beta m_{t-1}, (65)

where β=−0.25\beta=-0.25 in our experiments. We then clip the norm of the momentum direction independently for each sample:

g~t=min⁡(1,r‖mt‖2+ϵ)​mt,\widetilde{g}_{t}=\min\left(1,\frac{r}{\|m_{t}\|_{2}+\epsilon}\right)m_{t}, (66)

where r=2.5r=2.5 and ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. The clipped direction is decomposed into components parallel and orthogonal to the conditional velocity:

pt=g~t⊤​u¯t,yθ‖u¯t,yθ‖22+ϵ,g~t,∥=ptu¯θt,y,g~t,⟂=g~t−g~t,∥.p_{t}=\frac{\widetilde{g}_{t}^{\top}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}}{\|\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}\|_{2}^{2}+\epsilon},\qquad\widetilde{g}_{t,\parallel}=p_{t}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y},\qquad\widetilde{g}_{t,\perp}=\widetilde{g}_{t}-\widetilde{g}_{t,\parallel}. (67)

The APG-guided mean velocity is

u¯t,APGθ=u¯t,yθ+λ(g~t,⟂+ηg~t,∥).\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\mathrm{APG}}=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}+\lambda\left(\widetilde{g}_{t,\perp}+\eta\widetilde{g}_{t,\parallel}\right). (68)

We set η=0\eta=0, thereby removing the parallel component entirely. APG modifies only the mean velocity and retains the conditional branch’s predicted standard deviation.

APG+UCFG.

APG+UCFG replaces the fixed scale λ\lambda with a sample-wise adaptive scale selected to minimize the predicted uncertainty of the guided velocity. Unlike APG, APG+UCFG does not use reverse momentum. Instead, it clips the raw CFG direction using

ct=min⁡(1,r‖gt‖2+ϵ)c_{t}=\min\left(1,\frac{r}{\|g_{t}\|_{2}+\epsilon}\right) (69)

and removes its component parallel to the conditional velocity. Let

qt=(ct​gt)⊤​u¯t,yθ‖u¯t,yθ‖22+ϵ.q_{t}=\frac{(c_{t}g_{t})^{\top}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}}{\|\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}\|_{2}^{2}+\epsilon}. (70)

The resulting mean-guidance direction can be written as

dtu=ct​gt−qt​u¯t,yθ=(ct−qt)​u¯t,yθ−ct​u¯t,∅θ.d_{t}^{u}=c_{t}g_{t}-q_{t}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}=(c_{t}-q_{t})\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}-c_{t}\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}. (71)

Let σt,yθ​(𝐱¯t)\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) and σt,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) denote the element-wise standard deviations of the conditional and unconditional velocities, respectively. Applying the same clipping and projection coefficients to these standard deviations gives the uncertainty-guidance direction

dtσ=(ct−qt)​σt,yθ−ct​σt,∅θ.d_{t}^{\sigma}=(c_{t}-q_{t})\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}-c_{t}\sigma^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}. (72)

Therefore, the predicted standard deviation under scale λ\lambda is

σ~t,APG​(λ)=σt,yθ+λ​dtσ.\widetilde{\sigma}_{t,\mathrm{APG}}(\lambda)=\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}+\lambda d_{t}^{\sigma}. (73)

APG+UCFG then selects the sample-wise scale λ∗\lambda^{*} using the same variance-minimization and clamping procedure as UCFG in Appendix D, with dtσd_{t}^{\sigma} replacing the standard CFG uncertainty direction and λmax\lambda_{\max} serving as the upper bound. Finally, APG+UCFG returns the guided mean velocity u¯t,yθ+λ∗​dtu\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}+\lambda^{*}d_{t}^{u} and the standard-deviation surrogate σt,yθ+λ∗​dtσ\sigma^{\theta}_{t,y}+\lambda^{*}d_{t}^{\sigma}.

Appendix F Additional Results on Main Experiments

This section collects additional figures referenced by the main paper to complement the main experiments.

F.1 Uncertainty-Based Filtering

We evaluate whether uncertainty provides a useful reliability signal by progressively filtering out high-uncertainty generated samples and tracking changes in FID and precision/recall. Figure 9 summarizes the results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-128. Across datasets, UA-Flow exhibits a consistent precision-recall trade-off under filtering: removing the most uncertain samples increases precision while reducing recall.

CIFAR-10.

On CIFAR-10, the unfiltered sample quality is already high, so the precision gain from filtering is largely offset by the loss in recall, and FID tends to increase as the filtering ratio increases. We emphasize that this FID trend does not indicate that our uncertainty estimates degrade generation quality: the filtering experiment is designed to validate uncertainty as a per-sample reliability signal, not as a measure of the overall quality of the generated set. The consistent improvement in precision (i.e., fidelity) under filtering confirms that samples flagged as high-uncertainty by UA-Flow are indeed less reliable.

ImageNet-128.

On ImageNet-128, filtering more reliably improves fidelity: UA-Flow achieves lower FID and higher precision after filtering compared to AU and BayesDiff (with the expected decrease in recall). We include GenUnc as a reference baseline; it uses a domain-specific scalar uncertainty estimated in a CLIP embedding space, which is different in nature from element-wise uncertainty predicted by UA-Flow.

F.2 Uncertainty-Aware Guidance

F.2.1 Uncertainty-Aware Guidance (UG)

We sweep the UG scale ww under fixed classifier-free guidance (CFG) scales. As shown in Figures 10 and 4, increasing ww induces a consistent precision-recall trade-off across datasets: precision typically increases or peaks at an intermediate ww, while recall decreases as guidance becomes stronger. As a result, FID improves up to a dataset-dependent optimum, after which excessive guidance degrades performance. On CIFAR-10, where the baseline FID is already low, the same trade-off can translate into a FID increase at larger ww.

In Table 3(c), UG improves FID from 5.34 to 5.00 at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 on ImageNet-256. Because this margin is relatively small, we evaluate over 3 random seeds to confirm the improvement is not due to sampling randomness. As shown in Table 10, the FID gap persists across seeds with non-overlapping standard deviations (5.337±0.0425.337\pm 0.042 vs. 4.999±0.0474.999\pm 0.047), confirming that UG yields a consistent improvement at this operating point.

F.2.2 Uncertainty-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance (UCFG)

We compare standard CFG having scale λ\lambda with UCFG, which uses a step-wise adaptive scale λ∗\lambda^{*} clamped by λmax\lambda_{\max} on ImageNet-128. In Figure 11, increasing the fixed CFG scale eventually degrades both precision and recall, leading to a sharp rise in FID at large λ\lambda. UCFG shows smaller changes in precision/recall and less FID degradation as λmax\lambda_{\max} increases. The violin plots in Figure 12 show that λ∗\lambda^{*} is typically smaller in earlier sampling steps and larger in later steps. This pattern suggests that adaptive scaling limits over-guidance while the sample is still coarse and permits stronger guidance later in sampling.

Appendix G Supplementary Analyses

G.1 Uncertainty Evolution in BayesDiff and UA-Flow

Figures 13 and 14 compare the evolution of uncertainty maps over the sampling trajectory for BayesDiff and UA-Flow. Each figure shows the generated image (top), the estimated velocity uncertainty at intermediate steps (middle), and the propagated state uncertainty at the corresponding steps (bottom). Notably, both methods produce velocity uncertainty maps with clear spatial correlation, indicating that uncertainty concentrates in specific regions rather than being uniformly distributed. More specifically, velocity uncertainty obtained from UA-Flow is typically less noisy.

Despite using the same variance propagation rule (Equation 6), the propagated state uncertainty behaves very differently. For BayesDiff, the state uncertainty maps become largely unstructured and visually resemble noise, whereas UA-Flow yields state uncertainty maps that remain spatially coherent across steps. This behavior is consistent with Figure 15: BayesDiff exhibits a large uncertainty scale in the early sampling phase, and the corresponding early-step velocity uncertainty maps are also visibly noisy (e.g., step 12 in Figure 13). When such high-magnitude, noise-like velocity uncertainty is propagated, it can dominate the resulting state uncertainty and produce the unstructured, noise-like maps observed in Figure 13. In contrast, UA-Flow’s learned heteroscedastic velocity uncertainty is more spatially coherent, leading to propagated state uncertainty maps that remain structured.

G.2 Qualitative verification of uncertainty-based filtering

We next qualitatively assess whether UA-Flow’s sample-level uncertainty score distinguishes generated images by fidelity. To this end, we focus on two ImageNet-256 classes, hen and teddy_bear, and generate 1,000 samples per class using classifier-free guidance with scale λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 to show more realistic images. For each generated image, we compute the same scalar uncertainty score used for filtering in Section 4.2, then respectively select the 25 images with the highest uncertainty and lowest uncertainty.

Figures 16 and 17 show clear qualitative separation between uncertainty extremes. High-uncertainty samples frequently exhibit severe structural distortions and cluttered scenes. Low-uncertainty samples tend to be recognizable instances of the target class with clean textures and coherent global structure. These visual differences suggest higher perceptual fidelity in the low-uncertainty subset.

At the same time, the low-uncertainty subsets also reveal a fidelity-diversity trade-off. For hen, low-uncertainty samples are dominated by canonical compositions, typically close-up head/torso views on simple backgrounds. For teddy_bear, low-uncertainty samples often depict centered plush toys under relatively uniform backgrounds. In contrast, the high-uncertainty subsets span more diverse contexts, poses, and compositions, albeit with noticeably lower fidelity. Overall, these results provide qualitative evidence that UA-Flow uncertainty is aligned with sample-level quality, and that uncertainty-based filtering behaves as observed in Section 4.2: retaining low-uncertainty (high-fidelity) samples while implicitly reducing diversity.

G.3 Calibration analysis via reconstruction on validation images

Generative models lack ground-truth outputs since the model is designed to sample from the data distribution, not to reconstruct a specific target. We therefore use partially noised real images whose clean originals are known. These originals provide reference targets for an indirect calibration of the predicted endpoint variance.

Protocol.

We encode 500 each ImageNet images for calibration and validation to latent space 𝐳1∈ℝC×H×W\mathbf{z}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} via the Stable Diffusion autoencoder (C=4C=4 channels). For each t∈{0.5,0.7,0.9}t\in\{0.5,0.7,0.9\}, we sample noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and compute the noisy state 𝐳t=αt​𝐳1+βt​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}_{1}+\beta_{t}\epsilon. We then run the ODE from 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} at time tt to the predicted endpoint 𝐳^1\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{1} at time 1.01.0. For each method, we also compute the endpoint state uncertainty Var⁡[𝐳1∣𝐳t]\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{z}_{1}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]. The true latent 𝐳1\mathbf{z}_{1} serves as the ground-truth target for calibration.

We evaluate calibration using two standard metrics computed over all M=N×C×H×WM=N\times C\times H\times W scalar elements (images ×\times channels ×\times spatial locations):

  • •

    ECE (Expected Calibration Error): For each element ii, we compute the CDF value pi=Φ⁡((𝐳1,i−𝐳^1,i)/Var⁡[𝐳1,i])p_{i}=\Phi\!\bigl((\mathbf{z}_{1,i}-\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{1,i})/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{z}_{1,i}]}\bigr). Here, Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF. For a calibrated predictive distribution, the PIT values should be uniform on [0,1][0,1]. We evaluate their empirical CDF at B+1B+1 evenly spaced quantile levels qb=b/Bq_{b}=b/B, with b=0,…,Bb=0,\dots,B. We report ECE=1B+1​∑b=0B|F^​(qb)−qb|\text{ECE}=\frac{1}{B+1}\sum_{b=0}^{B}|\hat{F}(q_{b})-q_{b}|, where F^(q)=1M∑i𝟏[pi≤q]\hat{F}(q)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[p_{i}\leq q].

  • •

    Brier score for the 95% coverage event: We form the central Gaussian prediction interval IqI_{q} for each element at q=0.95q=0.95. We then compute 1M∑i(q−𝟏[𝐳1,i∈Iq])2\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i}(q-\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{z}_{1,i}\in I_{q}])^{2}. The event is whether the clean latent value lies inside this interval.

Post-hoc calibration is applied by fitting a scalar on a held-out calibration set (500 separate images) and rescaling the predicted variance. We use isotonic regression for the variance calibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018).

We compare UA-Flow against BayesDiff and AU. GenUnc is excluded because it produces a scalar uncertainty per sample, whereas UA-Flow, BayesDiff, and AU all produce per-component uncertainty, making them directly comparable. UA-Flow and BayesDiff are compared across all tt. AU is reported only at t=0.9t=0.9 since its uncertainty is defined only at the later steps of sampling.

Results.

Table 11 presents calibration results before and after post-hoc calibration. Before calibration, UA-Flow consistently outperforms BayesDiff across all noise levels, with the gap narrowing as tt increases. At t=0.9t=0.9, UA-Flow achieves ECE of 0.0277 and Brier of 0.1009, compared to 0.2386/0.9025 for BayesDiff and 0.0485/0.1782 for AU. At high tt, the noisy state retains most of the original signal, so the ODE effectively reconstructs the original image and calibration should be strong. At low tt, the signal is heavily corrupted and the trajectory resembles conditional generation, making calibration inherently harder. This provides a natural sanity check: calibration quality should improve monotonically with tt. As expected, UA-Flow’s calibration improves monotonically with tt. In contrast, BayesDiff shows nearly constant, higher ECE and Brier scores across the tested values of tt.

After post-hoc calibration via isotonic regression, ECE and Brier scores decrease for all methods. UA-Flow retains its advantage, reaching ECE of 0.0008 and Brier of 0.0481 at t=0.9t=0.9, compared to 0.0038/0.0505 for BayesDiff and 0.0012/0.0496 for AU. These results provide evidence that UA-Flow’s uncertainty estimates are meaningfully calibrated and serve as a reliable measure of sample quality beyond their practical usefulness for filtering.

G.4 Empirical validation of conditional–unconditional velocity correlation for UCFG

Uncertainty-aware classifier-free guidance (UCFG) combines conditional and unconditional predictions and approximates the variance of the extrapolated velocity by setting their correlation coefficient to ri=1r_{i}=1 (see Equation 13). To validate this assumption empirically, we measure the correlation between the predicted conditional and unconditional velocities along the sampling trajectory.

We generate 1,000 samples without CFG (i.e. λ=0\lambda=0) using the same sampling configuration as in our main experiments. At each intermediate sampling step, we evaluate the model twice at the current state: once with the class condition yy and once with the null condition ∅\varnothing, obtaining the element-wise mean velocities u¯t,yθ​(𝐱¯t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) and u¯t,∅θ​(𝐱¯t)\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}), respectively. To visualize their global relationship across time and spatial locations, we randomly subsample 10610^{6} element pairs (u¯t,∅θ,u¯t,yθ)\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,\varnothing},\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t,y}\big) from all steps and samples.

Figure 18 (left) shows an almost linear relationship between the unconditional and conditional velocities, with Pearson correlation r=0.993r=0.993 over the subsampled elements pooled across all sampling steps. Figure 18 (right) reports the per-step Pearson correlations, which are consistently close to 1.01.0 and exceed 0.980.98 at every step. Together, these results empirically support the approximation ri=1r_{i}=1 used to compute the UCFG velocity variance in Equation 13.

Appendix H Ablations on Uncertainty Estimation and Guidance

H.1 Ablations on the Uncertainty Estimation Pipeline

We vary one component at a time while otherwise following the filtering protocol in Section 4.2 (ImageNet-256, UA-Flow, no guidance). Figure 19 reports FID, precision, and recall.

Covariance approximation (Figure 19(a)).

We compare omitting the covariance term (Option 1), our one-probe JVP approximation (Option 2), and a 1010-sample Monte Carlo estimator (Option 3) (Kou et al., 2023). Omitting covariance performs worst, whereas Options 2 and 3 yield similar curves. We therefore use Option 2, which requires one probe rather than ten velocity evaluations per propagation step.

Variance term Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) (Figures 19(b) and 19(c)).

We compare the default predicted variance (σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2} with its sum with Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})), estimated using K=10K=10 Monte Carlo samples per step. Adding the latter leaves the filtering curves nearly unchanged despite a K×K\times cost. Across 10610^{6} locations and steps, it is small relative to the predicted term: Var⁡(u¯tθ​(𝐱t))≈0.036​(σtθ​(𝐱¯t))2+0.01\mathrm{Var}(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx 0.036\,(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}+0.01 (r=0.334r=0.334). We therefore omit it.

Number of Hutchinson probes SS (Figure 19(d)).

We approximate the covariance with Hutchinson’s estimator using S∈{1,2,4,8}S\in\{1,2,4,8\} probes. The resulting curves are nearly identical, so we use the single-probe setting S=1S=1.

Variance propagation method (Figure 19(e)).

We compare the default first-order Euler update with a Heun2 update that averages variance increments at the current and predicted next states. They yield closely matched curves; Heun2 provides only a small FID gain at high filtering ratios. We use Euler because it requires one fewer uncertainty evaluation per step.

Sparse uncertainty updates (Figure 20(a)).

We propagate uncertainty every 2, 4, or 8 sampling steps, rather than at every step. All settings yield consistent trends. We use every-four-step updates, matching BayesDiff (Kou et al., 2023) and reducing propagation evaluations by 4×4\times relative to per-step updates without affecting filtering quality.

Uncertainty aggregation ratio (Figure 20(b)).

We compare top-k%k\% aggregation of the uncertainty map (CVaRα\mathrm{CVaR}_{\alpha}) for k∈{1,5,10,25,50}%k\in\{1,5,10,25,50\}\%, using k=10%k=10\% by default. Results are stable for k∈[5%,25%]k\in[5\%,25\%]; 1%1\% emphasizes too few elements, whereas 50%50\% can dilute the tail signal.

H.2 Ablations on UG

Effect of f⁡(σ2)f(\sigma^{2}) (Figure 21(a)).

UG uses the gradient of a scalar function ff of the predicted variance. We compare mean_std, mean_variance (default), and mean_quadratic, which aggregate element-wise standard deviations, variances, and squared variances, respectively. mean_std and mean_variance yield similar curves, while mean_quadratic produces slightly sharper FID and precision peaks. We use mean_variance, indicating that UG is robust to the choice of ff.

Effect of guidance interval (Figure 21(b)).

We apply the UG correction in Equation 10 every 1, 2 (default), or 4 sampling steps. All intervals improve FID over the unguided baseline. Applying UG every step reaches its optimum at w=30w=30 but degrades at larger scales; the 2- and 4-step intervals shift the optimum upward without an apparent peak-out. We therefore apply UG every two steps.

H.3 Effect of the Bias-Correction Term Ut​(𝐱t,𝐱1)U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1})

The bias-correction term in Equation 2, Ut​(𝐱t,𝐱1):=u^t​(𝐱t)2−ut​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)2U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}):=\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2}, accounts for the gap between the marginal velocity estimate and the conditional target velocity. We train a matched UA-Flow checkpoint with Ut=0U_{t}=0 and evaluate filtering, UG, and UCFG on ImageNet-256. A stop-gradient velocity-prediction alternative was excluded because training was unstable.

Filtering and UG.

Without correction, filtering and UG still improve over the unguided baseline, with FID reductions comparable to the corrected model (filtering: Δ\Delta2.21 vs. Δ\Delta2.36; UG: Δ\Delta4.43 vs. Δ\Delta4.35). This suggests that their relative uncertainty rankings remain useful.

UCFG.

The correction is critical for UCFG. Without it, the best UCFG (FID 4.67±0.054.67\pm 0.05 at λmax=1.25\lambda_{\max}{=}1.25) does not surpass fixed CFG (FID 4.53±0.044.53\pm 0.04 at λ=0.75\lambda{=}0.75); with it, UCFG (FID 4.30±0.014.30\pm 0.01 at λmax=1.5\lambda_{\max}{=}1.5) outperforms fixed CFG (FID 4.48±0.014.48\pm 0.01 at λ=0.75\lambda{=}0.75). Figure 22 shows that removing the correction overestimates uncertainty early but produces slightly weaker adaptive CFG during the structure-forming intermediate phase, limiting UCFG’s benefit.

Appendix I Experiments on Non-Image Domains

To examine whether UA-Flow’s uncertainty estimation generalizes beyond image generation, we evaluate it on non-image domains where flow matching has been successfully applied.

I.1 2D Checkerboard

Setup.

We train a flow matching model on the 2D checkerboard distribution to verify that UA-Flow assigns high uncertainty to samples that fall outside the target support. The velocity network is a 3-layer MLP trained with batch size 4,096 for 100,000 iterations at learning rate 10−310^{-3}, followed by 100,000 fine-tuning iterations at learning rate 10−510^{-5}. At evaluation, we generate 10510^{5} samples using the Euler method with 100 NFE and compute the sample-level uncertainty score by reducing the propagated element-wise state variance to a scalar. We define coverage as the fraction of retained samples that fall inside the checkerboard grid.

Results.

Figure 23 visualizes the generated samples colored by their log state variance. High-uncertainty samples cluster near or outside the grid boundaries, while low-uncertainty samples concentrate well within the checkerboard cells. Quantitatively, the mean uncertainty score of samples outside the grid is 8.0×8.0\times higher than that of samples inside. This difference supports the use of the uncertainty score to identify out-of-support samples in this setting.

Table 13 reports coverage after filtering out the most uncertain samples. Without filtering, coverage is 95.7%. Removing the top 5% highest-uncertainty samples raises coverage to 98.8%, and removing 10% reaches 99.4%. These results provide evidence that UA-Flow’s uncertainty score can identify samples that deviate from the target support on a simple 2D distribution.

I.2 Time Series

Setup.

We consider a conditional time-series prediction task on synthetic sine-wave data. Each sequence is a noisy sine wave with frequency sampled uniformly from [0.5,2.0][0.5,2.0], amplitude from [0.5,1.5][0.5,1.5], and additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.010.01. Sequences are discretized at Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01. The first 50 steps serve as the conditional input and the subsequent 50 steps as the prediction target. The velocity network is a 1D UNet trained with batch size 4,096 for 40,000 iterations at learning rate 10−410^{-4}, followed by 10,000 fine-tuning iterations at learning rate 10−510^{-5}. At evaluation, we draw 1,000 random conditional inputs and generate 100 predictions per input using the Euler method with 100 NFE. The sample-level uncertainty score is computed by summing the propagated element-wise state variance over all predicted time steps.

Results.

Table 14 reports MSE between predicted and ground-truth trajectories after filtering out the most uncertain predictions. Filtering monotonically reduces MSE: removing the top 10% cuts error by 3.8×3.8\times (from 14.65×10−414.65\times 10^{-4} to 3.87×10−43.87\times 10^{-4}), and removing 90% yields a further reduction to 0.78×10−40.78\times 10^{-4}. Figure 24 illustrates this qualitatively: without filtering, some trajectories diverge from the ground truth, whereas the retained predictions after filtering closely track the true continuation. These results confirm that UA-Flow’s uncertainty serves as a reliable per-sample quality signal for conditional time-series generation, consistent with the filtering behavior observed in the image and 2D checkerboard experiments.

I.3 Robot Policy in Push-T Environment

Setup.

This preliminary study examines how chunk-level uncertainty relates to closed-loop outcomes in Push-T (Chi et al., 2025; Zhang and Gienger, 2024), where a policy pushes a T-shaped block to a target pose. We use a 1D UNet conditioned on a 76×7676\times 76 image and 2D agent position (observation horizon 2; prediction horizon 16; action chunk size 8), trained for 1,000 epochs with batch size 256 and learning rate 10−410^{-4}. At each decision step, we sum the propagated state variance across action dimensions to obtain an uncertainty score for one generated action chunk. We test whether this score can serve as an online abort signal, demonstrating the potential of UA-Flow’s uncertainty estimates for robotics applications.

Uncertainty-triggered early termination.

We terminate a rollout when its current chunk uncertainty exceeds a threshold τ\tau; Table 15 reports the retained rollouts among 1,000 trials. As τ\tau tightens, both the exclusion rate and retained success rate increase. At τ=0.001\tau=0.001, excluding 87.8%87.8\% of rollouts raises retained success from the 62.7%62.7\% baseline to 91.0%91.0\%.
